title_original: Can new regional funds help level up film production across England?
excerpt_original: ”I would like to think this is our moment in the sun. I feel that for all of the English regions.”

blocks.text: Source: Adobe Stock
Pictured clockwise from top left: Yorkshire, west of England, West Midlands, northeast, Greater Manchester, Liverpool and Cornwall

Andy Burnham wasted no time in throwing his weight behind devolving power away from London and backing “local industrial strategies” when he made his first speech to Parliament as UK prime minister in September.

The words from the former Manchester mayor, who is also the only prime minister to have previously been culture secretary, have been well received by England’s regional screen industries. “I’ll see what I’m saying in 12 months’ time, but I would like to think this is our moment in the sun,” says Screen Yorkshire chief executive Caroline Cooper Charles. “I feel that for all of the English regions.”
Source: Screen Yorkshire
Caroline Cooper Charles
UK producers still cluster around London and the southeast, where some 67% of the 838 production companies listed as members of UK producer trade group Pact are based.

In 2023-24, the most up-to-date figures available, 79% of the total funding amount from the BFI for development and production of features (via the Filmmaking Fund and the UK Global Screen Fund international co-production award) went to companies registered in London and the southeast, although many of these films shot across the UK.

However, over the past year, opportunities for production in the regions have been building, with several funds springing up for feature-­length film and TV series. Manchester has a £10.5m ($14m) production fund, the West of England Combined Authority (WECA) has a £4.5m ($6m) fund, and the West Midlands is launching a £6m ($8m) fund next year.

All three were made possible by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport’s Creative Places Growth Fund, through which six UK mayoral authorities with strength in the creative industries were awarded £25m ($33m) to administer between 2026 and 2029.

At the end of 2025, Screen Cornwall announced a £2.5m ($3.3m) fund, backed by Cornwall Council and private investors. Norfolk Screen also has a council-backed incentive in the works, which will be piloted on Sheree Folkson’s The Bright Side Running Club , due to shoot next spring. But enhanced production funding is just one piece of the jigsaw when it comes to levelling up opportunities for independent producers across England.
Commercial return

Screen Yorkshire was established in 2002, and founded the Yorkshire Content Fund in 2012. It is the longest-­running regional production fund in England and was set up initially with funding from the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF), which stopped being accessible to UK entities post-Brexit. It has not had top-up funding since a second round of ERDF funding in 2014 and continues to support production in Yorkshire by recouping on previous investments. Production companies must be registered in Yorkshire and Humber to access the funding, and producers must match the funding with the same amount of independent private finance.

“We invest, recoup, then reinvest,” explains Cooper Charles. “We are proud of the fact we don’t ask the public purse for money every year, which is stretched. On that basis, the drivers for the types of projects we invest in are slightly different [to other funds] because we have to focus on commercial return.”

Projects backed by Yorkshire Content Fund include Shane Meadows’ Chork and Molly Manners’ Extra Geography. Companies based in the region include Warp Films, Piers Tempest’s Tempo Productions and Hollie Bryan’s Cosmosquare Films. “We have become a bit of a beacon for feature films, as opposed to TV,” says Cooper Charles. “If you look at some of the other production funds, like Liverpool and North East Screen, the majority of their investments have been in TV.”

Its model means the fund does not have a consistent level of support year-on-year, but tends to back two or three projects annually with a maximum investment of £500,000 ($664,000) or 15% of the budget. To date, it has invested more than £24.4m ($32.2m) in local screen productions.

“One of the terms of our investment is that we need to match financing from commercial sources on identical terms,” continues Cooper Charles. “I always say to people, ‘If you want our money, the more aggressive the [recoupment terms of the] other money, the more aggressive we have to be, unfortunately.’”

The production fund has kept a steady flow of independent work in the region, but Screen Yorkshire acknowledges the challenges remain stark. It recently launched a three-year strategy to encourage local companies to be internationally competitive and retain intellectual property in the region, rather than rely on operating as a production service economy. Emerald Fennell’s Wuthering Heights for Warner Bros, Netflix’s Peaky Blinders: The Immortal Man and Netflix’s Tales Of The Unexpected series all shot recently in Yorkshire.

“One of the things that we’re critically aware of in the English regions is how much we are poor relations to the devolved nations,” says Cooper Charles. West Yorkshire alone has a bigger population than Northern Ireland, with the overall population of Yorkshire equal to Scotland; Northern Ireland Screen and Screen Scotland each have annual budgets of around £20m ($26.4m). Cooper Charles declines to comment on Screen Yorkshire’s exact annual budget but says it is less than a tenth of the nations’ budgets.

“All the producers [in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland] can still access those [UK-wide] pots of money from the BFI. That’s all available to them. But they’ve got a whole raft of [devolved nation-specific] funding available for things like business support, production support. There are production funds available in the English regions, but the other stuff isn’t generally there.”

Cooper Charles is hoping the strategy will go some way towards rectifying this with more targeted local business support. However, funding for Screen Yorkshire is inconsistent, and the piecemeal approach makes it hard to form long-term growth strategies. One third of funding is from the West Yorkshire Combined Authority, one third is from on­­going activity such as National Lottery support from the BFI Skills Clusters Fund (an initiative to plug skills gaps across the UK, with Screen Yorkshire leading on the scheme’s delivery for the north of England), and one third she says is pure “hustling”.
“I hustle for money in the way producers hustle for money,” notes Cooper Charles. “I know that pain.”

Screen Yorkshire’s neighbouring agency North East Screen has seen huge benefits from sustained investment in the region, courtesy of the BBC. In 2021, the broadcaster committed to spending at least £25m ($33m) over five years across the northeast, and has now increased this spend to £40m ($53m) by 2027.
Source: North East Screen
Alison Gwynn

North East Screen represents 12 local authority areas, including Newcastle upon Tyne and Northumberland. Alison Gwynn joined as chief executive of the then-­Northern Film and Media in 2017, when the agency was in dire straits. “I was brought in to either close the organisation or to reimagine what it could look like,” says Gwynn.
Consistent returns

Production spend across the past four years in the northeast has increased by 83%, with 1,419 more screen sector jobs created in this period. The crew base is estimated to have grown from 300 to more than 800. Gwynn says that as well as introducing newcomers to the industry, a lot of crew that had left the region have returned thanks to more sustainable work opportunities — in 2026, the region has some level of production across all 12 months for the first time. Production companies based in the region include a Sunderland branch of Fulwell Entertainment and Tina Gharavi’s Bridge + Tunnel Productions.

The region has been further propelled by a five-year £7.5m ($10m) local production fund, launched in 2023 and backed by Tees Valley Combined Authority and the North East Combined Authority, open to local and national companies. The fund is set up to be last money in, offering up to 20% of a project’s budget, capped at £500,000 ($664,000).

Nineteen projects have been supported so far — including BBC comedy series Smoggie Queens — but only two have been features: Jamie Childs’ Jackdaw and Gharavi’s Virginia Woolf’s Night & Day . Similarly, Liverpool City Region Production Fund launched with £2.8m ($3.7m) in 2019, and has backed only one feature to date, Babak Jalali’s A Town In Nova Scotia , which shot in January.
Source: SXSW London
‘Night And Day’

North East Screen has no preference between film and TV, according to Gwynn. “We’re looking for every single trainee on that production to be from our region, and a minimum of 50% of the crew should be from our region. For every pound invested, we expect a spend on supply chain of £10 [$13].”

Christopher Moll, a former head of film at Creative England from 2011-15 who helped set up the regional production funds in Liverpool and the northeast, and works as an advisor on the Manchester and West of England funds, says the economic impact that TV can demonstrate has made it more appealing in Liverpool and the northeast.

“In both of those instances, and with the new funds being launched, the monies are coming through the Mayoral Combined Authorities, and the combined authorities’ role is predominantly economic and infrastructural development,” notes Moll. “High-end TV is a key driver of those economic outputs.

“A smaller independent film with a four-to-five-week shoot is never going to punch with the same economic weight as a high-end TV show that’s going to film for 14 weeks as well as offer loads of training opportunities and the prospect of a recommission.

“In my experience, most of those [Mayoral Combined Authority] funding committees want to find a way to invest in independent film but they need clear reasons to offset the likely modest economic impacts,” adds Moll. “Is it a locally set story? Tick. Is local above-the-line talent involved? Is it developing a local production company? They recognise the value of film when it’s culturally specific. They understand that film, even more than TV, can deliver immense soft power to a region.”
Source: Screen File
Christopher Moll

He also cautions that much of the regional production funding could still be accessible to US studios and streamers, provided a UK-­registered company applies. “A good chunk of that money will hopefully go into shows and films from indigenous companies but everyone’s still in the inward investment game,” says Moll. “If a £4m [$5.3m]-plus per hour Netflix show comes along, it’s hard to resist.”
Public-private fund

Screen Cornwall, which represents the southwest England coastal county and the Isles of Scilly, has adopted a different model for its fund, which launched in late 2025. It is the only production fund backed by both public and private money in the UK, taking inspiration from Ireland’s local authority and commercial investor-backed Western Region Audiovisual Producers (WRAP) Fund.

Screen Cornwall Equity Production Investment has £2.5m ($3.3m) to invest by 2028. The first project backed by the fund was Richard Eyre’s upcoming The Housekeeper . “The reason we set up the initiative was to drive those people who are considering Cornwall to consider it seriously, and to drive local companies to build their businesses and grow the ecosystem overall,” says Laura Giles, managing director at Screen Cornwall. “We need more production companies and producers making work that’s travelling beyond Cornwall’s borders.”

The fund is backed by Cornwall Council and private investors. Screen Cornwall is a registered community interest company, which Giles says has helped it appeal to high-net-worth individuals with a philanthropic mindset, some with personal connections to the area.

A production company does not have to be based in Cornwall to apply, with the focus on spend in the region. There is a requirement for 50% of financing to be locked in before Screen Cornwall will come on board, though “we have wiggle room” for a local company, notes Giles.
A strong focus on sustainable production is also baked into the Cornish fund’s criteria. “The assets we have are all green and blue and could be heavily impacted by bad practice,” explains Giles.

Notable independent film producers based in the region include Denzil Monk’s Bosena ( Rose Of Nevada ) and Dean Puckett of Grasp The Nettle Films ( Grand Theft Hamlet ). Monk has recently launched Field Work, a talent development programme for emerging producers in the region that is backed by the BFI’s Creative Challenge Fund for decentralising training and development work.

Giles feels more needs to be done to break down the geographic barriers that prevent further local companies from establishing themselves. “We work a lot with [early career scheme] BFI Network in the southwest and that’s positive. But it’s tough for a producer in the rural and coastal regions. That job is so reliant not just on your creative relationships, but your business and financial relationships, and the reality is those exist in places that are a very long way to travel and very expensive to get to.”

She adds: “For emerging producers, there might be something more about a travel and festival/market attendance support that would allow them to build their network and connections outside the region.”

Giles describes the recent announcement of WECA’s £4.5m ($6m) Greenlight West fund as “very positive” for the whole of England’s southwest. She hopes it will stimulate production in Cornwall, with the possibility of a project being able to access both funds if shooting across locations in both areas.

Greenlight West supports productions in Bristol, Bath, northeast Somerset and south Gloucestershire. The region is known as the home of Aardman Animations and is a major international hub for natural history programming. Two routes are open for production funding: one for local companies and one for companies from outside the region that promise high local spend. Non-­recoupable grants of £100,000-£500,000 ($133,000-$664,000) are available via both routes, with the first round of fund recipients to be announced in December.
Source: Freia Turland
Annabel Smith

Annabel Smith, director of strategic partnerships and stakeholders at WECA, says the main challenge for the region is “converting activity into a sustainable pipeline. We attract fantastic productions to the region [including Disney+ series Rivals and Jonatan Etzler’s Bad Apples ]. We’ve got strong infrastructure but, like many places outside London, the challenge is to create that more consistent pipeline of work over time and maintain that regular flow of production activity.”

The first dedicated post-­production regional fund will soon be launched in the west of England, offering grants of £50,000-£200,000 ($66,000-$265,000) for production work done in the region, and open to projects that have shot both inside and outside the area.

Greenlight West’s funding is being administered from within the local mayoral authority, as is the case with the £10.5m ($14m) Greater Manchester fund — which means the funds will not be administered by sector specialists, and there is no established support system or databases for crew, facilities, locations and skills. In 2011, the UK government consolidated several regional screen agencies into Creative England (now Creative UK), and these three regions still do not have fully fledged screen agencies. The creation of such departments is understood to be under discussion in these regions.

The BFI has attempted to decentralise some of the National Lottery support it administers through its Skills Clusters and the Creative Challenge Fund. A BFI spokesperson said: “Ensuring a greater spread of funding across the UK continues to be a key priority for the BFI. Films supported through the BFI Filmmaking Fund often tell distinctively UK stories which convey a very strong sense of place, with recent examples including The Incomer (Scotland), Out There (Wales) and I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning (Birmingham).

“While producers awarded funding often have companies registered in London, that has no bearing on where production takes place, and we know a considerable amount of production on the UK-shot films we support takes place outside London and the southeast.”
Source: Hugo Hastings
Laura Giles
However, local screen agencies would like central government to unlock even more devolved funding. “Fiscal devolution is a major opportunity in our part of the world,” says Smith.
“The more bespoke support that rural and coastal places can design for themselves, the better. We know what our talent needs,” says Giles.

For several years, Screen Yorkshire has been making its case to culture secretary Lisa Nandy for a tax incentive uplift for projects shooting outside the London Metropolitan Area. “It’s still on our wishlist,” confirms Screen Yorkshire’s Cooper Charles.

She emphasises that a hyperlocal approach is not just about economic value — it benefits the audience. “People respond to different landscapes and settings and perspectives,” she says. “We’re all just a bit bored of seeing London again and again and again on our screens.”
A bigger picture: Regional production funds in England

Greater Manchester Production Fund Launched: June 2026 Amount per project: £50,000-£750,000 ($66,000-$996,000), up to 20% of the total budget Overall pot: £10.5m ($14m), rolling for three years Key requirements: UK-based production company; broadcaster interest; key financiers in place (for film) Funding structure: Grant funding for Manchester-based companies of up to £500,000 ($664,000); recoupable equity investment for local companies requesting more than £500,000 ($664,000) or non-local companies

Greenlight West Launched: September 2026 Amount per project: £100,000-£500,000 ($133,000-$664,000), up to 20% of the total budget Overall pot: £4.5m ($6m), rolling for three years Key requirements: UK-based production company; significant production activity in the region if a non-local company; credible route to market Funding structure: Non-recoupable grant

Liverpool City Region Production Fund Launched: March 2019 Amount per project: £100,000-£500,000 ($133,000-$664,000), up to 20% of the total budget Overall pot: £2.8m ($3.7m), rolling Key requirements: UK-based production company; at least 50% of finance in place; demonstrable route to market; staffed production base in the region for the duration of the shoot Funding structure: Recoupable equity investment with net profits participation

North East Screen Production Fund Launched: September 2023 Amount per project: £50,000-£500,000 ($66,000‑$664,000), up to 20% of the total budget Overall pot: £7.5m ($10m), rolling for five years Key requirements: UK-based production company; local co-producer if a non-local company; staffed production base in the region for the duration of a shoot Funding structure: Recoupable equity investment with net profits participation

Screen Cornwall Equity Production Investment Launched: November 2025 Amount per project: Up to £500,000 ($664,000) Overall pot: £2.5m ($3.3m), rolling for three years Key requirements: UK production company; projects shoot in Cornwall or the Isles of Scilly; 4:1 qualifying spend ratio; at least 50% of finance in place Funding structure: Recoupable as senior equity with a share of net profits

West Midlands Content Production Fund Launched: Early 2027 Amount per project: £100,000-£600,000 ($133,000-$796,000) Overall pot: £6m ($8m) Key requirements: UK-based production company; demonstrable economic, employment and sector benefits in the region Funding structure: Recoupable or non-recoupable grant determined on a project-by-project basis

Yorkshire Content Fund Launched: February 2012 Amount per project: Up to £500,000 ($664,000) Overall pot: No fixed pot, rolling Key requirements: The project must be managed by a registered SME in Yorkshire and Humber; demonstrable market value (ie, sales agent or distribution in place); matched with private equity investment Funding structure: Co-invest in identical terms to private sector investment; can match investment in equity, gap finance, mezzanine finance, cashflowing against the UK tax credit, broadcast or distributor contracts
